question: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-week history of abdominal cramps, vomiting, and constipation. He also reports having to urinate frequently and occasional leg pain. He has had similar episodes in the past. He has hypertension and peptic ulcer disease. Current medications include captopril and ranitidine. He appears depressed. Physical examination shows weakness in the extremities. Abdominal examination shows mild epigastric tenderness. There is no rebound or guarding. He has a restricted affect. Laboratory studies show elevated serum parathyroid hormone levels; serum calcium is 14.2 mg/dL. Abdominal ultrasonography shows multiple small calculi in the right kidney. Which of the following is most likely to provide rapid relief in this patient?

options.opb: Reduction of dietary intake of calcium
options.opc: Normal saline and intravenous furosemide therapy
options.opd: Normal saline and intravenous fentanyl therapy
options.ope: Normal saline and intravenous calcitonin therapy

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Elevated serum calcium" -> "Increased risk of kidney stones" -> "Frequent urination and abdominal cramps" -> "Possible hypercalcemia-related symptoms" -> "Normal saline and intravenous furosemide therapy" -> "Increased renal excretion of calcium" -> "Rapid relief of symptoms" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Elevated serum parathyroid hormone" -> "Increased serum calcium levels" -> "Symptoms of hypercalcemia" -> "Frequent urination and leg pain" -> "Normal saline and intravenous furosemide therapy" -> "Decreased serum calcium" -> "Improved symptoms" -> 80%

CHAIN: "Hypercalcemia" -> "Abdominal cramps and vomiting" -> "Increased calcium in urine" -> "Formation of kidney stones" -> "Normal saline and intravenous furosemide therapy" -> "Promotes calcium excretion" -> "Rapid symptom relief" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Patient with hypercalcemia" -> "Symptoms include weakness and abdominal pain" -> "Need for rapid intervention" -> "Normal saline and intravenous furosemide therapy" -> "Effective in managing hypercalcemia" -> "Improvement in clinical status" -> 88%
analysis: The patient presents with symptoms consistent with hypercalcemia, including abdominal cramps, vomiting, constipation, and frequent urination. The elevated serum calcium level (14.2 mg/dL) and elevated parathyroid hormone levels suggest primary hyperparathyroidism or a parathyroid-related condition. In cases of severe hypercalcemia, rapid treatment is necessary to lower calcium levels and alleviate symptoms. Normal saline and intravenous furosemide therapy (option c) is a common approach to manage hypercalcemia, as it helps to promote renal excretion of calcium. Other options, such as intravenous pamidronate or calcitonin, may also lower calcium levels but are not as immediate in effect as hydration and diuresis. Therefore, option c is the most likely to provide rapid relief in this patient.
